## From a paired change to a repeated-response model

This article is for a reader who can already distinguish a visit mean from a
paired change in the [first analysis](frequentist-long-getting-started.html).
Some familiarity with the idea of regression is helpful. The new question is:
**how can we estimate mean change while describing the dependence between
several responses from the same participant?** We first study one outcome,
one population, and three visits. Groups and adjustment come later.

A paired t analysis models the distribution of one difference per person. A
repeated-response model instead models the original score at each visit. Its
mean structure describes differences between visit means, and its covariance
structure describes how values from the same person move together. These are
separate modeling choices. An ordinary regression treating every measurement
as independent would ignore the participant grouping.

The target is mean **Month 6 minus Baseline best-corrected visual acuity
(BCVA)**, measured as ETDRS letter score, in adults receiving follow-up for
diabetic macular edema (DME). More letters mean better measured acuity. Positive
change describes a visual-acuity gain; without a comparator it does not identify
a treatment effect. This tutorial is not a treatment recommendation or a
model-selection rule for every retinal study.

## A new study, large enough for the demonstration

The entry dataset is useful for hand calculation. We now generate a different
synthetic DME cohort of 80 adults, each with one protocol-designated eligible
study eye and measurements at baseline, Month 3 and Month 6. Both eyes are
assumed eligible in this synthetic population; the protocol randomly designates
one right or left eye before any response is generated. The fellow eye is excluded.
`eye_map` retains the one-to-one patient/eye mapping. Independent sampling units
are people; one study eye per person makes the number of independent eyes equal
to the number of people. A study using both eyes would need an additional
correlation structure, not `strict_id = FALSE`.

The illustrative population letter-score means are 57, 61 and 65. A shared
patient deviation (SD 7.5 letters) induces repeated-measure correlation; separate
measurement errors have SD 3.2 letters. We round to whole letter counts, then
check that this seeded sample lies in a plausible interior teaching window.
No value is clipped or replaced. The Gaussian mixed model is a working
approximation to these discrete scores, not a claim that all acuity data are
unbounded Gaussian measurements. These generating values are invented for
teaching, not calibrated treatment effects.

```{r first-model-data}
library(MIRA)
set.seed(731017)
n <- 80L
eye_map <- data.frame(
  participant_id = sprintf("DM%03d", seq_len(n)),
  study_eye = sample(c("R", "L"), n, replace = TRUE)
)
eye_map$study_eye_id <- paste(eye_map$participant_id, eye_map$study_eye, sep = "_")
retina_complete <- data.frame(study_eye_id = eye_map$study_eye_id)
participant_deviation <- rnorm(n, 0, 7.5)
retina_complete$bcva_t0 <- round(57 + participant_deviation + rnorm(n, 0, 3.2))
retina_complete$bcva_t3 <- round(61 + participant_deviation + rnorm(n, 0, 3.2))
retina_complete$bcva_t6 <- round(65 + participant_deviation + rnorm(n, 0, 3.2))
visits <- c("bcva_t0", "bcva_t3", "bcva_t6")
labels <- c("Baseline", "Month 3", "Month 6")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(eye_map$participant_id),
  !anyDuplicated(eye_map$study_eye_id),
  identical(retina_complete$study_eye_id, eye_map$study_eye_id),
  all(is.finite(as.matrix(retina_complete[visits]))),
  all(as.matrix(retina_complete[visits]) > 10 & as.matrix(retina_complete[visits]) < 95))
head(retina_complete)
```

We retain the familiar wide input: one row per participant. The 80 people
contribute 240 measurements. The labels identify visits; they do not supply
individual elapsed times to MIRA. The primary model treats visit as a factor,
so it estimates a separate population mean for each occasion rather than
forcing change to be linear in months.

## Make one model request and inspect the primary fit

The change from a descriptive call is `analyses = "model"`. This requests
MIRA's implemented model bundle; there is no public selector that fits only
the random-intercept model. Our learning sequence reads one component first,
without pretending that the computation excludes the other modules.
`covariates = character(0)` states that this demonstration has no adjustment.
Supplying `analyses` overrides the optional logical switches. The five-letter
`stable_threshold` only illustrates an observed-change classification band;
it is not a validated minimal clinically important difference (MCID), treatment
success rule or measurement-error model.

```{r first-model-fit}
analysis <- mira_info_long(
  retina_complete, id = "study_eye_id", time_vars = visits,
  time_labels = labels, outcomes = "bcva",
  covariates = character(0), analyses = "model",
  improvement_direction = "higher", stable_threshold = 5,
  alpha = 0.05, p_adjust_method = "holm", verbose = FALSE
)
analysis$model[c("converged", "singular", "warnings", "error")]
stopifnot(!is.null(analysis$model$fitted_model))
primary <- analysis$model$fitted_model
formula(primary)
```

The printed formula is `value ~ time_factor + (1 | patient_factor)`.
`value` is the study-eye BCVA letter score, including baseline as a response. The fixed
visit term describes population means. The random intercept allows each
participant to be consistently above or below those means. In notation,
`BCVA(i, j) = visit_mean(j) + participant_deviation(i) + error(i, j)`.
The participant deviations are assumed independent across people, normally
distributed with mean zero, and independent of the normally distributed
errors. The residual variance is constant in this primary specification.

Two measurements from one person share the random intercept. Under this
model their covariance is the participant-intercept variance, while each
measurement's variance also includes residual variance. This accounts for
dependence without treating a participant-specific deviation as an observed
covariate or an individual treatment effect. The primary model is fitted by
REML; the global nested-model likelihood tests stored elsewhere use ML.

`converged` concerns optimization and `singular` concerns unsupported random
variation. Neither establishes suitable residuals, correct missingness
assumptions, or scientific adequacy. If no fit is available, stop the
interpretation and inspect `error`, rather than filling in an estimate.

## Which observations were actually used?

Read the model frame rather than assuming that every input row contributed.
The assertions below independently construct expected participant-by-visit
keys from the wide table. They verify identities as well as the count.

```{r first-model-sample}
frame <- model.frame(primary)
used_keys <- paste(as.character(frame$patient_factor),
                   as.character(frame$time_factor), sep = "::")
expected_keys <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(visits), function(k) {
  observed <- is.finite(retina_complete[[visits[[k]]]])
  paste(retina_complete$study_eye_id[observed], labels[[k]], sep = "::")
}), use.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(used_keys), setequal(used_keys, expected_keys))
sample_audit <- data.frame(participants = length(unique(frame$patient_factor)),
                          measurements = nrow(frame),
                          complete_profiles = sum(complete.cases(retina_complete[visits])))
knitr::kable(sample_audit, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Primary model sample: people and measurements are different units.")
```

All 80 participants have all three values in this particular dataset. With
incomplete response histories, eligible finite measurements can contribute
under the model's assumptions; a missing required predictor can exclude a
person's measurements. A mixed model does not impute missing values. The
[missing-data article](frequentist-long-missing-data.html) distinguishes
availability, complete profiles, MAR, and MCAR before such a model is applied.

## Read one mean difference

The `emmeans` component turns the fitted model into model-based means and
contrasts. We select the named final-minus-baseline contrast. MIRA-owned
numeric columns can be outcome-prefixed; the table's `mira_metric_names`
attribute tells us their actual names. The following visible helper creates a
display copy and also works for unprefixed structural keys.

```{r first-model-contrast}
metric_table <- function(x, columns) {
  mapping <- attr(x, "mira_metric_names")
  actual <- columns
  mapped <- columns %in% names(mapping)
  actual[mapped] <- unname(mapping[columns[mapped]])
  stopifnot(all(actual %in% names(x)))
  answer <- x[, actual, drop = FALSE]
  names(answer) <- columns
  answer
}
emmeans_result <- analysis$advanced_tests$emmeans
stopifnot(isTRUE(emmeans_result$performed),
          is.data.frame(emmeans_result$baseline_final$tidy))
endpoint <- metric_table(emmeans_result$baseline_final$tidy,
  c("contrast", "estimate", "lower.CL", "upper.CL", "p_raw", "p_primary"))
endpoint <- endpoint[endpoint$contrast == "final - baseline", , drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(nrow(endpoint) == 1L,
          all(is.finite(unlist(endpoint[c("estimate", "lower.CL", "upper.CL")]))))
display <- endpoint[c("contrast", "estimate", "lower.CL", "upper.CL", "p_primary")]
display$p_primary <- format.pval(display$p_primary, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
knitr::kable(display, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Month 6 minus Baseline BCVA in ETDRS letters: model-based mean change and pointwise 95% interval.")
```

The estimated mean difference is `r sprintf("%.2f", endpoint$estimate)` ETDRS letters,
with a 95% pointwise interval from `r sprintf("%.2f", endpoint$lower.CL)` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", endpoint$upper.CL)`. Positive values mean higher scores at
Month 6. The interval quantifies uncertainty about a population mean
difference, rather than the range of individual changes. A 95% confidence
procedure covers the fixed target in 95% of repeated samples under its
assumptions; it does not assign a 95% frequentist probability that the fixed
target lies inside this particular interval.

The p-value tests zero mean difference under the fitted model. It is not the
probability that the null hypothesis is true or a measure of clinical
importance. This `baseline_final` family contains one comparison, so Holm
leaves its p-value unchanged. It does not adjust across the other families
that the bundle also computes. A plan choosing one primary contrast should
state that choice before inspecting results.

For this balanced, complete, unadjusted design, the fitted mean difference
equals the mean of the raw paired differences. Verify the estimate from the
wide data rather than by reading another model field. Agreement of estimates
does not imply equal standard errors for every covariance specification.

```{r first-model-oracle}
raw_change <- retina_complete$bcva_t6 - retina_complete$bcva_t0
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(endpoint$estimate, mean(raw_change), tolerance = 1e-8)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(endpoint$p_raw, endpoint$p_primary)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(raw_paired_mean = mean(raw_change),
                       model_mean_difference = endpoint$estimate),
             digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "An independent estimate check from the original paired scores.")
```

## Check the model, retain the result, then extend the question

Residual checks ask whether the covariance and distributional assumptions are
plausible. They complement the computational flags. Here the data were
generated with a random intercept and constant Gaussian residual variation;
real data may require a different scientific strategy.

```{r first-model-residuals, fig.cap="Conditional residuals from 80 participants and 240 measurements, in ETDRS letters. These diagnostics describe the primary model; they are not confidence intervals or individual predictions."}
local({
  previous <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
  on.exit(par(previous))
  residual <- residuals(primary)
  plot(fitted(primary), residual,
       xlab = "Fitted study-eye BCVA (ETDRS letters)", ylab = "Conditional residual (letters)")
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
  qqnorm(residual, main = "Conditional residuals")
  qqline(residual)
})
```

Save the already interpreted result; the report reuses it without refitting.
The temporary directory is suitable for a reproducible tutorial. A real
project should choose a controlled archive location and retain the data,
protocol, software versions, and source code with appropriate access controls.

```{r first-model-save}
saved_result <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(analysis, saved_result)
bundle <- mira_report_freq_long(x = analysis,
  output_dir = tempfile("mira-first-bcva-model-"), format = "html",
  render = FALSE, open = FALSE)
stopifnot(file.exists(saved_result), file.exists(bundle$results_manifest),
          !any(bundle$rendered))
```

The source-only bundle is an archive, not a finished HTML report. Detailed
export and rendering contracts are in the
[reporting article](frequentist-long-reporting.html). The next
[model article](frequentist-long-advanced-models.html) introduces a new
two-arm dataset with scientific adjustment, contrasts between changes,
alternative covariance structures, and partially usable module results.
That is a new question and configuration, rather than another reading of
these same 80 participants. The engine authors explain the
[mixed-model formula](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/lmer.html) and
[model-based marginal means](https://rvlenth.github.io/emmeans/articles/basics.html)
in more depth.


The [DRCR Retina Network visual-acuity measurement protocol](https://public.jaeb.org/drcrnet/stdy/149)
provides the ophthalmic measurement context. Our simulated means, variability,
follow-up schedule and five-letter teaching band are independent design choices,
not results or eligibility rules copied from that protocol.
